_readme: Treatment products — serums, ampoules, spot treatments and hydrocolloid patches — consumed by build-kbeauty-pages.cjs. Same contract as the rest of the library: cosmetic structure-function wording, no invented INCI or percentages, no medical advice, honest caveats.

products.name: Acne Pimple Master Patch
products.whatItIs: A sheet of hydrocolloid dots in three sizes, and the single product that turned spot patches from a Korean pharmacy habit into a global one. Hydrocolloid is a wound-dressing material: it swells as it draws fluid out of a blemish that has already opened, going opaque white as it fills. There are no actives here at all — no salicylic acid, no tea tree, no niacinamide. The design is purely physical: cover the spot, flatten it, keep your fingers off it.
products.whoItSuits: Best on the specific spot that has come to a head or been picked open, because that is the only situation where hydrocolloid has anything to absorb. Suits oily, combination and blemish-prone skin, and it is tolerable for sensitive skin precisely because nothing is delivered into it. It does very little for a deep closed bump under the surface, and nothing at all for blackheads.
products.howToUse: Cleanse and dry the area properly first — the patch will not grip damp or freshly moisturised skin. Press on the smallest dot that covers the spot, leave it six hours or overnight, and lift it off once the centre has turned white and opaque. It goes on bare skin, before serums and moisturiser, not on top of them.
products.watchOut: It is a dressing, not a treatment, and the marketing is content to let people assume otherwise. On unbroken skin it mainly stops you picking. The adhesive can leave a pink ring on reactive skin, and using one on the same patch of face night after night gets irritating. Painful, recurring cystic breakouts are a conversation for a clinician, not a sticker.

products.name: Clear Fit Master Patch
products.whatItIs: The daytime sibling of the original master patch: thinner, flatter and far less visible, with a bevelled edge that sits close enough to the skin to disappear under makeup. Same hydrocolloid principle, same absence of actives — the trade is that a thinner layer holds less fluid. All the dots come in one modest size rather than a graded set, which suits small spots and makes it awkward on large ones.
products.whoItSuits: For anyone who wants a patch they can wear to work or on camera. Oily, combination and blemish-prone skin get the most from it, and there is no active load to worry sensitive skin. If your spot is actively weeping or large, the original thicker patch will hold more and last longer. Not the one to buy if you only ever patch overnight — the extra invisibility is wasted.
products.howToUse: Same routine as any hydrocolloid: clean, dry, bare skin first, then press and leave. Under makeup, apply the patch before foundation and dab product over it rather than dragging a brush across the edge. Replace it when the centre clouds over, which on a busy spot can be well before the day is out.
products.watchOut: Thin means less absorbent. On a spot that is genuinely leaking, it saturates fast and the edges start lifting, which is worse than not patching at all. The invisibility is relative — under bright light and on deeper skin tones a matte disc still catches the eye. And, as with every patch, it does nothing for the closed bumps that never surface.

products.name: The Vitamin C 23 Serum
products.whatItIs: A high-strength pure L-ascorbic acid serum in a thick, slightly syrupy base, and the strongest rung of COSRX's vitamin C ladder — the same line runs a gentler low-percentage version for people who cannot take this one. Pure ascorbic acid is the best-evidenced form of topical vitamin C for the look of tone and brightness, but it is also the most unstable and the most likely to sting. Nothing about this formula hides that.
products.whoItSuits: For normal, oily or combination skin that already tolerates actives and wants the strongest well-documented form of vitamin C rather than a comfortable derivative. Good for the look of uneven tone, dullness and lingering post-blemish marks. Sensitive, rosacea-prone or barrier-compromised skin should not start here — the lower-strength version of the same serum exists for exactly that reason.
products.howToUse: Morning, on clean dry skin, before anything else — a few drops is plenty and more is genuinely wasteful. Wait a minute, then moisturiser and sunscreen. Sunscreen is not optional with this one; vitamin C is a poor substitute for it and a good partner to it. Start two or three mornings a week and build up only if your skin stays calm.
products.watchOut: It stings for most people on the first applications, and a burn that does not settle within a few minutes means stop, not persevere. Ascorbic acid oxidises: as the serum turns from pale to amber it is losing potency, so buy small and finish it. Do not layer it with strong exfoliating acids or a retinoid in the same session. The tacky finish also pills under some sunscreens.

products.name: Centella Blemish Ampule
products.whatItIs: A thin, watery centella ampoule built for skin that is irritated rather than dry — the 진정 (jinjeong, soothing) end of the COSRX range rather than the exfoliating end. Centella asiatica extract and its isolated fractions carry the formula, with very little else doing anything: no acids, no fragrance-forward finish, no heavy emollients. It is deliberately unexciting, which is the point of a product you reach for when your face is already annoyed.
products.whoItSuits: Oily, combination and blemish-prone skin that flushes easily, and sensitive skin looking for something to layer on a bad week. It sits well over an acid or retinoid routine on the nights you skip them. If your main problem is dryness rather than redness, this will not do much — there is almost no moisturising weight in the bottle.
products.howToUse: After cleansing and toner, before your moisturiser, morning or evening. A few drops pressed over the whole face, or dabbed just where you are red. It absorbs in seconds and layers under anything. Nothing here conflicts with actives, so it works fine as the calming layer on nights you use something stronger.
products.watchOut: The word blemish in the name does a lot of unearned work — centella is a soothing ingredient with reasonable support for the appearance of redness, not something that clears breakouts. Expect it to make an angry face look calmer, not fewer. It is also so light that it needs a moisturiser over it, and the slight tackiness annoys some people under sunscreen.

products.name: Full Fit Propolis Light Ampoule
products.whatItIs: A propolis extract ampoule with a honeyed, faintly amber look and a texture to match — light in name, decidedly sticky in practice. Propolis is the resinous material bees collect and process; in skincare it is used as a comforting, mildly antioxidant humectant and it is one of the ingredients most associated with the glowing, wet-looking finish people buy Korean skincare for. The extract content is high enough that the product smells and behaves like what it is.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and normal skin that wants dewiness without an occlusive layer, and combination skin in winter. It flatters dull, tired-looking skin more than almost anything else at this price. Anyone with a known reaction to bee products — propolis, honey, royal jelly — should leave it alone, and very oily skin will find the tack unpleasant by mid-afternoon.
products.howToUse: Evening suits it best, after toner and before moisturiser, though a thin layer in the morning under a light sunscreen works if you like the finish. Two or three drops pressed rather than rubbed in. Give it a minute to set before anything goes on top, or the stickiness drags.
products.watchOut: Propolis is a reasonably common contact allergen, so patch-test properly rather than going straight to the face — anyone who reacts to bee stings or honey should be especially careful. The finish is genuinely tacky and can pill under certain sunscreens. And propolis products vary wildly in extract quality between brands, so reviews of one are not evidence about another.

products.name: BHA Blackhead Power Liquid
products.whatItIs: A leave-on BHA treatment built on betaine salicylate rather than straight salicylic acid, alongside willow bark extract. Betaine salicylate is milder gram for gram, which is why the number on the label looks high next to a Western BHA — the two are not directly comparable. The liquid is thin and slightly slippery, sits closer to a watery serum than a toner, and has been a fixture in oily-skin routines for over a decade.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin with congestion around the nose, chin and forehead, and anyone whose skin finds a strong salicylic acid too much. Normal skin can use it a few times a week for texture. Dry, sensitive or barrier-compromised skin should approach cautiously if at all, and it is not the product for closed cystic bumps or for skin already using a nightly retinoid.
products.howToUse: Evening, on clean dry skin after toner, before serums and moisturiser. A thin layer over the congested areas rather than the whole face. Start twice a week and build to alternate nights if your skin stays comfortable. Daily sunscreen matters more once you are exfoliating regularly.
products.watchOut: Blackheads in the name promises more than any leave-on liquid delivers — sebaceous filaments refill, and they are normal anatomy rather than a fault to be eliminated. The milder acid also means slower results than people expect from the percentage. It can be drying on the cheeks, and stacking it with a retinoid or an AHA on the same night is the usual route to a compromised barrier.

products.name: Glow Serum: Propolis + Niacinamide
products.whatItIs: A propolis-heavy serum with niacinamide as the second lead, and one of the products that carried this brand from a Korean-market curiosity to a global shelf staple. The propolis gives the honeyed slip and the wet-looking finish; the niacinamide is the better-evidenced half, with reasonable support for the appearance of tone, texture and pore visibility. It is a simple formula sold at an unusually honest price for what is in it.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and normal skin wanting dewiness, and combination skin that finds most brightening serums drying. Sensitive skin generally tolerates it, with the caveat that niacinamide makes some people flush. Anyone with a bee-product allergy should skip it entirely. Very oily skin often finds the propolis tack unpleasant, and there are lighter niacinamide serums for that.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, once or twice a day. Two to three drops pressed into damp skin, then seal with a cream — on its own it is not a moisturiser. In the morning, give it a full minute before sunscreen so it stops feeling sticky. It layers happily with almost anything except a high-strength ascorbic acid in the same sitting.
products.watchOut: The stickiness is real and no amount of technique removes it. Propolis is a recognised contact allergen, so patch-test rather than trust the brand's gentle positioning. Niacinamide at meaningful levels causes a warm flush in a minority of people — if that is you, it will not fade with persistence. And glow here means a light-reflecting hydrated finish, not a change in pigment.

products.name: Revive Serum: Ginseng + Snail Mucin
products.whatItIs: The brand's 한방 (hanbang, traditional Korean herbal medicine) angle applied to a modern serum: ginseng root extract paired with snail secretion filtrate in a bouncy, slightly gel-like base. Ginseng is the heritage ingredient in Korean skincare and carries most of the brand's storytelling; snail mucin is the part doing the visible work, holding water and leaving the plumped, cushioned finish it is known for. Comfortable, cheap for the category, and pleasantly herbal.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, normal and mature skin looking for hydration with a bit of bounce, and anyone drawn to the herbal end of Korean skincare. Combination skin can use it at night. Snail mucin is mollusc-derived, so vegans and anyone with a shellfish or mollusc sensitivity should avoid it. Oily skin prone to congestion sometimes finds the film heavy under sunscreen.
products.howToUse: Evening is the natural home for it, after toner and before a cream, though it works in the morning if you like a dewy base. Two or three drops on damp skin, pressed in and given a moment to set. It layers under a sleeping mask well. Nothing in it conflicts with acids or retinoids used on other nights.
products.watchOut: Ginseng's reputation in skincare rests far more on centuries of traditional use than on strong clinical work, and the anti-ageing framing around it is thinner than the marketing suggests. Snail mucin is a good humectant with a hard-earned fan base, but the repair language attached to it across the whole category is over-claimed. The scent is distinctly herbal and not everyone likes it.

products.name: Glow Deep Serum: Rice + Alpha Arbutin
products.whatItIs: Rice extract, the oldest brightening story in Korean skincare, paired with alpha arbutin, one of the better-tolerated modern tone ingredients. Arbutin is a slow, gentle worker on the look of dark marks and uneven tone; rice contributes a soft-focus, slightly milky finish that flatters skin immediately. The texture is thin and disappears fast, which is a large part of why this became the brand's most reached-for serum after the sunscreen.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, dry and combination skin working on the appearance of post-blemish marks and general unevenness, and a reasonable first step for anyone who found vitamin C too irritating. Oily skin will like the finish. It is not a fast fix for stubborn melasma, and anyone dealing with that should be talking to a clinician rather than shopping — topical brighteners alone rarely settle it.
products.howToUse: Morning or night after toner, before moisturiser. Two to three drops over the whole face rather than spot-treating, since uneven tone is rarely as local as it looks. In the morning it belongs under sunscreen, and sunscreen is the part that actually decides whether any of this holds. Give it eight to twelve weeks before judging.
products.watchOut: Arbutin is slow and modest, and without daily sun protection it is effectively pointless — new pigment forms faster than any cosmetic ingredient fades the look of the old. The name suggests something deeper-acting than it is. Some people also confuse this category with skin lightening, which it is not. Persistent or spreading pigmentation deserves a clinician's opinion, not a fourth serum.

products.name: Peach 70 Niacin Serum
products.whatItIs: A niacinamide serum in a peach extract base, following the same naming convention the brand uses across its range: the big number counts the botanical extract, not the active. The texture is light and slightly milky with a soft peach scent, and the whole thing is engineered around feel as much as function. Niacinamide is the ingredient with the actual evidence behind it, sensibly supported for the appearance of tone, texture and pore visibility.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and mildly dry skin that wants a comfortable everyday niacinamide rather than a clinical one. Good for the look of dullness and rough texture. People who flush from niacinamide will flush from this too. If you dislike scented skincare, the peach note is noticeable enough to be a dealbreaker, and fragrance-free niacinamide serums are easy to find.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, once or twice a day. Two or three drops is enough for the whole face. It layers under sunscreen without pilling, which is not true of every serum at this price. If you also use a high-strength ascorbic acid, put them at opposite ends of the day rather than stacking them.
products.watchOut: The number in the name is a marketing convention, not a potency claim — a high percentage of fruit extract is mostly water with fruit in it, and it tells you nothing about how much niacinamide is present. The peach scent is pronounced. And niacinamide, while well supported, works slowly and subtly; anyone expecting a visible change in a fortnight will be disappointed.

products.name: Niacinamide 10% + TXA 4% Serum
products.whatItIs: A tone-focused serum pairing a high level of niacinamide with tranexamic acid, both stated on the front of the bottle. Tranexamic acid arrived in skincare from medicine, where the oral and injected forms have a real evidence base for stubborn pigmentation; the topical version is a much newer and thinner literature. Niacinamide is the steadier partner. The texture is light and non-greasy, which makes it easy to slot into an existing routine.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and oily skin working on the appearance of post-blemish marks and diffuse unevenness. It suits people who found vitamin C too unstable or too irritating. Very sensitive skin should be careful — ten per cent niacinamide is enough to make some faces warm and pink. Anyone with diagnosed melasma should treat this as a supporting player and see a clinician about the rest.
products.howToUse: Once daily to start, after toner and before moisturiser, morning or evening. A few drops over the whole face. Sunscreen every day is what makes or breaks any pigmentation routine, and it matters more than which serum you chose. Give it a couple of months of consistent use before deciding whether it earns its place.
products.watchOut: Niacinamide at ten per cent is above the level most people need and above the level some can tolerate — the flushing is not something you push through. Topical tranexamic acid is promising but the published work is far smaller than the oral evidence people quote at it, and the two are not interchangeable. Melasma in particular is a medical problem with a stubborn habit of returning; a clinician should lead.

products.name: Azelaic Acid 10 Hyaluron Redness Soothing Serum
products.whatItIs: One of the few Korean cosmetic serums built openly around azelaic acid, buffered with hyaluronic acid to take the edge off. Azelaic acid is unusual in this category: it has genuine clinical history at prescription strengths for redness and blemish-prone skin, and it does not increase sun sensitivity the way an AHA does. At the cosmetic level used here it is a gentler, slower version of that. The texture is a light lotion rather than a watery drop.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive, combination and blemish-prone skin dealing with the look of persistent redness and lingering marks. It is a reasonable option for people who cannot tolerate acids or retinoids. Anyone with diagnosed rosacea should be having this conversation with a clinician, who can prescribe the higher strengths that the evidence actually rests on. Very dry skin may need extra moisturiser over the top.
products.howToUse: Evening to start, after toner, before moisturiser, every other night for the first fortnight. A pea-sized amount for the whole face. It can move to twice daily once tolerated. It does not conflict with sunscreen or niacinamide, and it is one of the few actives that plays reasonably well with a retinoid — though not on the same night at first.
products.watchOut: Ten per cent sits well below the prescription strengths the clinical evidence is built on, so temper expectations accordingly. Azelaic acid has a real tendency to pill under sunscreen or makeup, and a mild tingling in the first weeks is common. It is also slow. Persistent facial redness has several possible causes, some of which need diagnosis rather than a serum.

products.name: Heartleaf 80% Daily Relief Ampoule
products.whatItIs: The ampoule version of the brand's signature 어성초 (eoseongcho, heartleaf) formula, thicker and more concentrated than the toner that made the ingredient famous outside Korea. Houttuynia cordata has a long history in Korean and Chinese herbal use and has become the default soothing botanical of the current K-beauty wave. The texture is a light gel that sinks in without residue, aimed squarely at skin that is reactive, congested or freshly annoyed by something else.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive, oily and blemish-prone skin having a bad week, and anyone whose face goes pink easily. It sits well as the calming layer in a routine that also uses acids or retinoids on other nights. Dry skin will need a proper cream over it — this adds almost no lasting moisture. If heartleaf has irritated you before, the higher extract content here will not be kinder.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning or night. A few drops pressed over the whole face, or concentrated on the red areas. It layers under sunscreen cleanly. On a genuinely irritated day, use it alone under a bland moisturiser and pause everything else until things settle.
products.watchOut: An extract percentage on the front of a bottle measures how much of the water phase is a botanical infusion, not how potent it is — 80 per cent of a weak extract is still a weak extract. Heartleaf's soothing reputation rests mainly on traditional use and a modest amount of laboratory work rather than strong human trials. The green, slightly earthy smell puts some people off entirely.

products.name: Madagascar Centella Ampoule
products.whatItIs: A deliberately minimal ampoule: centella asiatica extract from Madagascar and very little else, sold in a large dropper bottle at a price that makes people use it generously. Centella is the most-studied soothing botanical in Korean skincare, and its isolated fractions have decent support for the appearance of redness and irritation. The formula's whole argument is subtraction — no fragrance, no essential oils, nothing extra for reactive skin to catch on.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive and easily-flushed skin, oily skin that reacts to richer soothing products, and anyone running a routine with acids or retinoids who needs a neutral layer on the off nights. Normal skin can use it as a light hydrating step. Dry skin should not expect it to moisturise — there is almost nothing occlusive in the bottle, and a cream on top is mandatory.
products.howToUse: After cleansing and toner, before moisturiser, morning and evening if you like. Several drops pressed into the face, which is easy given the bottle size. It absorbs almost instantly and layers under sunscreen without pilling. Useful as a first-aid step: a generous layer under a plain moisturiser on a day when your skin has had enough.
products.watchOut: This is centella in water, and its ceiling is correspondingly low — it makes an irritated face look calmer and does not do anything else. The large bottle encourages using far more than any layer needs. Centella is well tolerated but not universally: a small number of people react to it, and being a plant extract does not exempt it. Patch-test if you are reactive.

products.name: Madagascar Centella Tone Brightening Capsule Ampoule
products.whatItIs: The brand's tone-focused ampoule, suspending visible capsules in a centella base with niacinamide as the working ingredient. The capsules dissolve as you spread the product, which is a texture experience more than a delivery breakthrough. Underneath the theatre it is a sensible, low-irritation brightening option: niacinamide for the look of tone and unevenness, centella keeping the whole thing comfortable for skin that reacts to stronger actives.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and oily skin working on the appearance of dullness and post-blemish marks, particularly anyone who found vitamin C or acids too much. Sensitive skin usually copes, though niacinamide flushing is always possible. It is not the choice for deep-set pigmentation or melasma — those need a clinician's plan and a great deal of sun protection rather than a gentler ampoule.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, once or twice daily. A few drops warmed briefly between the fingers so the capsules break down, then pressed over the face. Morning use belongs under sunscreen. Consistency matters more than quantity here — two months of daily use tells you more than a heavy hand for a fortnight.
products.watchOut: The capsules are a texture gimmick and the marketing leans on them harder than the formula deserves. Brightening in Korean cosmetics means the look of a more even, luminous tone, not lightening skin colour, and the translation confuses people constantly. Results from niacinamide are slow and modest at best. Anyone with pigmentation that is spreading or changing should see a clinician.

products.name: AHA BHA PHA 30 Days Miracle Serum
products.whatItIs: The serum in the brand's best-known range: three acid families at cosmetic levels alongside tea tree water, aimed at oily and congested skin. The three-acid approach is more about covering different solubilities than about strength — the AHA works on the surface, the BHA is oil-soluble enough to get into a pore, the PHA is the gentlest of the set. The whole line is built around the same promise and sold as a set.
products.whoItSuits: Oily, combination and congested skin that wants a mild everyday exfoliating step rather than a weekly strong one. Reasonable for the look of rough texture and visible pores. Dry, sensitive or barrier-compromised skin should stay away, and so should anyone already using a nightly retinoid. If you have inflamed cystic breakouts, this is not the product and a clinician is the better call.
products.howToUse: Evening, after toner, before moisturiser. Start twice a week and build slowly, watching for tightness or stinging. Follow with a plain moisturiser and use sunscreen daily — exfoliating acids make that non-negotiable. Do not run the toner, cleanser and serum from this line all at once; pick one exfoliating step and keep the rest bland.
products.watchOut: The 30 days in the name is a marketing promise no leave-on cosmetic can make good on, and the miracle framing sets people up to over-use the whole range. Buying the matching cleanser, toner, serum and cream is the most common route to an irritated, stripped barrier we see in this category. Tea tree is also a known contact allergen for a minority.

products.name: Snail Truecica Miracle Repair Serum
products.whatItIs: The gentler half of the brand's range, pairing snail secretion filtrate with the centella fraction it markets as Truecica. Snail mucin is a well-liked humectant that leaves skin looking plump and dewy; the centella side is there for the appearance of redness. Together they make a comfortable, slightly tacky serum aimed at people whose skin has been through an acid-heavy phase and now looks tired rather than congested.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, normal and combination skin recovering the look of comfort after a period of over-exfoliation, and sensitive skin that gets on with snail mucin. Good alongside, not instead of, sun protection when you are watching post-blemish marks fade. It is mollusc-derived, so not for vegans. Very oily skin often finds the film heavier than it wants in summer.
products.howToUse: Evening after toner, before moisturiser, or morning if you like the dewy finish under makeup. A few drops on slightly damp skin, pressed in and allowed a moment to set. It layers well over a soothing ampoule and under a cream. Nothing in it conflicts with actives used on other nights.
products.watchOut: Repair and miracle are cosmetic marketing, not descriptions of what happens — snail mucin hydrates and comforts, and the evidence for anything beyond that is thin. Post-blemish marks fade largely on their own with time and diligent sunscreen, which is unglamorous but true. The texture is genuinely sticky, and mollusc-derived ingredients are worth patch-testing if you react to shellfish.

products.name: DIVE-IN Low Molecular Hyaluronic Acid Serum
products.whatItIs: A plain, fragrance-light hyaluronic acid serum that became a bestseller by being unobjectionable. Several molecular weights of hyaluronic acid, a watery gel texture, no acids, no strong botanicals, nothing that argues with anything else in a routine. It is the product people are pointed to when their skin is irritated and they need a hydrating layer that cannot make things worse. That modesty is the entire selling point.
products.whoItSuits: Every skin type, which is unusual and mostly a function of how little is in it. Particularly useful for dehydrated oily skin that wants water without oil, and for sensitive skin between stronger products. It is not a moisturiser and will disappoint anyone expecting one. If your skin is dry rather than dehydrated, you need the cream more than you need this.
products.howToUse: Onto damp skin after cleansing or toner, morning and evening, then seal with a moisturiser within a minute or two. Applying humectants to dry skin in dry air is the classic mistake — the water has to come from somewhere. Two or three drops. It layers under sunscreen and makeup without pilling, which is half its popularity.
products.watchOut: Humectants without something over them can leave skin feeling tighter in cold, dry air, which is the opposite of the point. The low molecular weight penetration story is stretched well past what the evidence supports, and no hyaluronic acid serum is doing anything dramatic below the surface. This is a good cheap hydrator; it is not worth paying a premium over any other decent one.

products.name: PDRN Pink Peptide Serum
products.whatItIs: The product that pushed PDRN — polydeoxyribonucleotide, a salmon-derived DNA fragment ingredient — from Korean clinics into home routines. Injectable PDRN has been used in aesthetic medicine for years, and the cosmetic version borrows its reputation wholesale. The serum itself is a light pink fluid with peptides alongside the headline ingredient, pleasant to use and heavily marketed on the strength of the clinic association rather than on topical data.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination, dry and mature skin curious about the ingredient and comfortable paying for the novelty. It is a decent light hydrating serum with a comfortable finish and no obvious irritants. It is salmon-derived, so not for vegans or anyone avoiding fish-derived ingredients. If your budget is finite, a retinoid and a sunscreen have far more evidence behind them for the look of ageing.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning or evening. A few drops over the face and neck. It layers without pilling and does not conflict with retinoids or acids used at other times. As with anything sold on firmness and elasticity claims, judge it over months rather than weeks, and keep sunscreen as the constant.
products.watchOut: The evidence gap here is the whole story: the interesting PDRN research is on injected material delivered below the skin surface, and none of it transfers automatically to a molecule applied on top. Ask what a topical trial has actually shown before paying clinic prices at home. It is expensive for a light serum, and the ingredient is currently in a hype cycle that will outlast the data.

products.name: Green Tea Seed Serum
products.whatItIs: The long-running hydrating serum built around green tea from the brand's own Jeju plantations, and one of the products most Korean consumers can picture without prompting. Green tea polyphenols have reasonable antioxidant credentials in the laboratory; in a serum like this the practical benefit is a light, non-greasy hydration layer with a clean green scent. It has been reformulated across several generations, each keeping the name and changing the texture.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and mildly dry skin wanting an everyday hydrating step that vanishes under makeup, and oily skin that dislikes heavier serums. It suits people who want something pleasant rather than something active. It will not do much for pigmentation, texture or lines — this is a hydration and comfort product wearing an antioxidant story.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning and evening. Two or three drops on damp skin. It is light enough to layer under a richer cream in winter, and light enough to work alone in summer for oily skin. Follow the morning application with sunscreen, since antioxidants support sun protection rather than replace it.
products.watchOut: Successive generations of this serum have differed enough in texture and formula that online reviews may describe a product you cannot buy any more — check the packaging generation before trusting a rave. The green tea scent is noticeable. And the antioxidant framing outruns the evidence for what a rinse-off-adjacent leave-on layer of tea extract does on human skin over time.

products.name: Retinol Cica Repair Ampoule
products.whatItIs: A retinol ampoule buffered with centella, which is the standard Korean approach to retinoids: pair the active with a soothing botanical and pitch it at people nervous about irritation. Retinol has the strongest evidence of any cosmetic ingredient for the look of fine lines and texture, and it is also the one most likely to make skin flake, sting and go red in the first weeks. The opaque, air-restricting packaging matters, because retinol degrades in light.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination, oily and mature skin ready to start a retinoid and wanting a gentle entry point. Useful for the appearance of fine lines, rough texture and congestion. Not for sensitive or barrier-compromised skin without a slow build, and not for anyone pregnant or breastfeeding — that is a conversation for a clinician, and the general advice is to avoid retinoids entirely.
products.howToUse: Evening only, on dry skin after cleansing, starting two nights a week. A small amount, avoiding the eye area and the corners of the nose. Moisturiser over the top, or under it if you need to buffer. Build up over weeks, not days. Daily sunscreen is mandatory — retinoids raise sun sensitivity and undo themselves without it.
products.watchOut: The cica in the name softens the marketing, not the retinoid — expect flaking and tightness in the first fortnight regardless. Do not use it on the same night as acids, strong vitamin C or a second retinoid product. Retinol also degrades with light and air, so a jar or a clear bottle would be a red flag, and even good packaging does not make an old tube potent.

products.name: Time Revolution Night Repair Ampoule
products.whatItIs: A ferment-led night ampoule and one of the longest-running products in Korean mass skincare, sold from the beginning as an accessible answer to a famous Western night serum. Bifida ferment lysate is the headline: a bacterial ferment filtrate used across the category for the look of resilience and smoothness. The texture is a light amber fluid that sinks in fast. It has been reformulated and renamed across several generations, each marked on the box.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, dry, combination and mature skin wanting a comfortable evening ampoule with a hydrating, smoothing finish. It is an easy product to tolerate and layers under anything. It is not an active in the sense a retinoid or an acid is, so anyone hoping to change texture or pigment will need something else in the routine. Fragrance-sensitive skin should check the current pack.
products.howToUse: Evening, after toner, before moisturiser or a sleeping mask. A few drops pressed over face and neck. It suits the nights you are not using a retinoid, and it also works as a buffering layer under one if your skin is sensitive. Give it a season rather than a fortnight before deciding.
products.watchOut: The comparison to a famous imported night serum has sold this ampoule for years, and the two formulas are not the same product at a different price — treat the dupe framing as marketing. The line has also changed formula and numbering repeatedly, so older reviews may describe something quite different. It is fragranced, and ferment-heavy formulas do not suit every reactive skin.

products.name: Cicapair Serum
products.whatItIs: The serum in the range that made tiger grass a global marketing term — tiger grass being centella asiatica, the same plant behind half the soothing products in Korean skincare. This is the straightforward member of the family: a light, fast-absorbing serum aimed at the appearance of redness and reactivity, without the colour-correcting pigment that the better-known cream in the line carries. Dermatology-adjacent branding, department-store pricing, a genuinely well-studied lead ingredient.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive and combination skin that flushes easily, and normal or dry skin that wants a calming layer without weight. It sits well in a routine that uses stronger actives on alternate nights. Anyone already using an inexpensive centella ampoule is unlikely to see a difference worth the price gap. Fragrance-avoidant skin should read the current pack carefully.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning or evening. A few drops pressed over the face, concentrating where you are red. It layers cleanly under sunscreen. On a day when your skin has been over-treated, use it under a bland moisturiser and pause acids and retinoids until things look settled.
products.watchOut: Tiger grass is centella with a better name, and it is the same ingredient sold for a fifth of the price elsewhere. The Cicapair line also spans a green colour-correcting cream, a mask and this serum, so reviews routinely describe the wrong product. Fragrance is present in parts of the range, which is an odd choice for products aimed at reactive skin.

products.name: Ceramidin Serum
products.whatItIs: The serum step of a barrier-focused range built around ceramides, the lipids that make up part of the skin's own outer structure. Topical ceramides are one of the better-supported ideas in moisturising: they suit dry, flaky and easily-irritated skin, and they work best in company rather than alone. The serum is lighter than the cream and liquid in the same line, which makes it a layering product rather than the whole answer to dryness.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, flaky and sensitive skin, and mature skin that has become less comfortable over time. Useful in winter and in air conditioning. Oily skin rarely needs it. If you are buying one product from this range, the cream is the more logical purchase — a ceramide serum without an occlusive over it is doing half a job, which the range's own structure quietly admits.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, evening especially. Apply to slightly damp skin and follow with a cream to seal it — this is the step where that instruction genuinely matters. Morning use under sunscreen is fine for very dry skin. It layers well over a hydrating serum and under a sleeping mask in cold weather.
products.watchOut: Ceramides are lipids and want an occlusive layer above them; used alone as your last step, a light serum will underdeliver and you will blame the ceramides. The range is also large and repetitive, with the liquid, serum and cream covering much the same ground at three price points. Marketing around ceramide ratios in cosmetics generally outruns what the finished formula can demonstrate.

products.name: Wonder Releaf Centella Serum Unscented
products.whatItIs: A centella serum with panthenol support, sold unscented and aimed at the reactive-skin end of the market. The formula is deliberately short and free of essential oils, which is the right instinct for a product whose entire job is not provoking anything. Texture is a light, slightly slippery gel that sinks in without residue. It is the sort of formula that does not photograph well and works quietly, which is the correct trade for this category.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive, dry and normal skin looking for a soothing layer with slightly more substance than a watery centella ampoule. It suits people building a minimal routine after over-treating their skin. Combination skin can use it year-round. Anyone whose main complaint is congestion or texture will find it beside the point — nothing here exfoliates or resurfaces.
products.howToUse: After cleansing and toner, before moisturiser, morning or evening. A few drops pressed rather than rubbed. It layers under sunscreen without pilling and pairs sensibly with a plain ceramide cream. On a badly irritated day, keep the routine to cleanser, this and a moisturiser, and leave the actives in the cupboard.
products.watchOut: Worth knowing about the brand rather than the serum: independent testing found one of its sunscreens fell well short of the SPF on the label, and the product was withdrawn. That was a sunscreen and not this formula, but it is a fair reason to hold the brand's own claims loosely. Unscented also does not always mean fragrance-free — read the current list.

products.name: Freshly Juiced Vitamin Drop
products.whatItIs: A low-strength pure ascorbic acid serum, pitched for years as the beginner's vitamin C and still one of the most sensible entry points in the category. Pure ascorbic acid is the form with the strongest evidence behind it for the appearance of tone and brightness; at this level the trade is less irritation for slower, subtler change. The texture is slightly thick and takes a moment to sink in, which is typical of a water-based ascorbic acid formula.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, dry and combination skin starting with vitamin C, and reasonably sensitive skin that cannot take a high-strength serum. Good for the look of dullness and lingering post-blemish marks. Anyone already comfortable on a stronger ascorbic acid will find this underpowered. It is not the answer to deep pigmentation, and it is not a substitute for sunscreen in any routine.
products.howToUse: Morning, on clean dry skin, before moisturiser and sunscreen. A few drops, then a minute to settle. Start every other day and go daily if your skin is comfortable. Keep it somewhere cool and dark. Do not pair it with a retinoid or strong acids in the same session; put them at opposite ends of the day.
products.watchOut: Even at this level it tingles on many faces, so the gentle positioning is relative rather than absolute. Ascorbic acid oxidises once opened — as the liquid darkens towards yellow-brown it is losing strength, and a bottle you nurse for a year is doing very little by the end. Buy the small size, use it daily, and replace it rather than economising.

products.name: Green Tangerine Vita C Dark Spot Serum
products.whatItIs: A tone-focused serum built on green tangerine extract from Jeju — the unripe fruit, which the brand markets as the more concentrated stage — rather than on a high dose of pure ascorbic acid. That makes it a gentler, more stable proposition than a traditional vitamin C serum, and a considerably slower one. The texture is light and non-sticky with a clear citrus scent, and it has been a fixture of Korean drugstore brightening for years.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination, oily and dry skin looking for the look of a more even tone without the sting and instability of pure vitamin C. A sensible option for people who tried ascorbic acid and gave up. Anyone with established pigmentation who wants visible change will need more than this, plus rigorous sun protection, and probably a clinician's input if it is melasma.
products.howToUse: Morning or evening after toner, before moisturiser. A few drops over the whole face rather than dabbing at individual marks. Morning use goes under sunscreen, which is the part of any tone routine that actually decides the outcome. Give it two to three months of daily use before forming a view.
products.watchOut: Extract-led vitamin C is not the same proposition as ascorbic acid, and the label leans on the vitamin C association harder than the formula earns. Expect subtle change at best. The citrus scent is noticeable, so check the current ingredient list if fragrance is an issue for you. Dark spot in a product name is a cosmetic tone claim, not a promise of removal.

products.name: Dark Spot Correcting Glow Serum
products.whatItIs: A niacinamide serum with squalane and fruit extracts, and the product that carried a small brand into international rotation. Niacinamide is the working ingredient and one of the few with a decent evidence base for the appearance of uneven tone, texture and pore visibility; squalane keeps the finish comfortable rather than dry. The texture is a light lotion that leaves a soft sheen, which is where the glow in the name comes from.
products.whoItSuits: Combination, oily and normal skin working on the look of post-blemish marks and general unevenness, and dry skin that finds most tone serums stripping. It is a reasonable everyday step rather than a corrective one. People who flush from niacinamide should be careful, and anyone with a bee-product allergy should check the current formula, as the brand has used honey-derived ingredients across its range.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning or evening — once daily is enough to start. Two or three drops over the whole face. Morning use goes under sunscreen. Judge it over a couple of months; niacinamide is a slow ingredient and no serum in this category changes anything in a fortnight.
products.watchOut: Correcting is doing heavy lifting in that name. Niacinamide softens the look of marks gradually and does nothing for pigment that keeps being re-triggered by unprotected sun exposure. The brand has adjusted this formula over the years, so a review from a few seasons ago may not describe the bottle you receive. Flushing from niacinamide is common enough to plan for.

products.name: Madecassoside Ampoule
products.whatItIs: A cheap, plain ampoule built around madecassoside, the isolated centella fraction with the most laboratory work behind it for the appearance of irritated skin. There is very little else in the bottle and the texture is thin and watery — closer to a hydrating toner than the rich concentrate the word 앰플 (aempul, ampoule) implies. In Korea that word marks a marketing tier rather than a concentration standard, which is worth knowing before you pay for one.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive and easily-flushed skin on a budget, oily skin that dislikes richer soothing products, and anyone who wants a neutral layer between actives. Normal and combination skin can use it as a light hydrating step. Dry skin will need a proper cream over it. If you already own a centella ampoule, this does the same job and there is no reason to own two.
products.howToUse: After toner, before moisturiser, morning or evening. A few drops pressed over the face or applied just to the red areas. It absorbs quickly and layers under sunscreen without pilling. On an irritated day, use it generously under a bland moisturiser and pause exfoliants until your skin looks settled.
products.watchOut: It is inexpensive and correspondingly limited — a soothing layer, not a treatment, and it does nothing for texture, pigment or breakouts. The ampoule label sets up expectations of a concentrate that the watery texture does not meet. Centella and its fractions are well tolerated by most people but not all, so patch-test if your skin has a history of reacting to plant extracts.

products.name: Reedle Shot 100
products.whatItIs: The product that made spicule ampoules a mainstream category. Spicules are microscopic mineral-like needles derived from freshwater sponge, suspended in a centella-based fluid; they sit on the skin and create very shallow micro-channels, which is why the brand talks about needles at home. The numbering — 100, 300, 700 — marks increasing spicule intensity rather than a percentage of anything, and 100 is the entry point for a reason.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and oily skin that is otherwise healthy, curious about the sensation and willing to build up slowly. It suits people chasing the look of smoother texture. It is emphatically not for sensitive, reactive or barrier-compromised skin, not for anyone with active inflamed breakouts or broken skin, and not for anyone already running a retinoid or acids more than occasionally.
products.howToUse: Evening, on clean dry skin, starting once or twice a week. A small amount patted — never rubbed hard — then left a few minutes before a plain moisturiser. Skip everything else active that night. Sunscreen the next day matters, since freshly abraded skin is more vulnerable. Stop entirely if stinging persists past the first minutes.
products.watchOut: This is a physical abrasive dressed as a technology. Heat and prickling are described as normal, which makes it hard for users to tell irritation from the intended sensation — a poor situation for any product. The at-home needling framing implies clinical microneedling results that a topical cannot deliver. Anyone considering it for scarring should see a clinician about the actual procedure instead.

products.name: First Care Activating Serum
products.whatItIs: Korea's best-known luxury first step, sold at home as 윤조에센스 (yunjo essence) and abroad under a longer English name. It sits on the 한방 (hanbang) tradition of herbal medicine, with a ginseng-led botanical complex and a deliberately theatrical herbal scent. The texture is a light oil-in-water fluid that goes on before toner rather than after — a sequencing convention the brand essentially invented and the rest of the market copied.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, dry, mature and combination skin that enjoys the ritual and can absorb the price. It genuinely feels lovely and leaves skin looking supple straight away. Sensitive skin and anyone who avoids fragrance should stay well clear — this is one of the most heavily scented products in mainstream Korean skincare. Oily skin rarely needs the extra layer at all.
products.howToUse: First step after cleansing, on damp skin, before toner and everything else, morning and evening. Two or three pumps warmed in the palms and pressed into the face. Follow with your usual routine. The brand's sequencing instruction is unusual and worth following if you are paying this much, if only to judge it on its own terms.
products.watchOut: The price buys heritage, packaging and scent as much as formula, and the first step concept is a brand convention rather than a requirement of skin physiology — nothing is activated by going first. Ginseng's skincare reputation rests largely on traditional use rather than robust clinical work. The fragrance load is high, which makes it a poor choice for reactive skin regardless of budget.
